title: Horizontal Logic — McKinsey Executive Brief
description: A white-field executive-summary layout built on the McKinsey horizontal-logic principle: a declarative action-title sentence above a hairline rule, three numbered evidence columns, and an 8pt italic source line at the bottom-left. Unlike generic corporate grids, every structural element enforces conclusion-first argumentation rather than labelling a topic.
philosophy: This template exists for analysts and partners who believe the slide title must state the so-what, not describe the subject. It rejects gradients, icon libraries, and decorative chrome in favour of typographic discipline and strict logical hierarchy. The three-column parity structure forces balanced evidence and prevents the rhetorical sleight-of-hand of the single supporting bullet. It is built for rooms where senior audiences read the action title before the presenter speaks and challenge the structure immediately.
goodFor: Board-ready strategy summaries anchored by a single declarative conclusion
Consulting deliverables where a McKinsey or BCG horizontal-logic structure is expected
Executive briefings where audiences skim action titles before listening
Situation-complication-resolution readouts with three parallel evidence streams
avoidFor: Visual storytelling slides requiring a single dominant hero image
Sales decks that rely on emotional hooks and large product photography
Data-heavy dashboard pages with six or more chart panels
Workshop or facilitation slides where open whitespace and prompts are needed
author: harness

examples.promptCore: A white-field cover of institutional authority — the mood is a senior partner dropping a bound brief on a boardroom table: deliberate, spare, and slightly intimidating in its restraint. Compositional rhythm is asymmetric and top-anchored; the title mass descends through a hairline rule into an expanse of white silence that signals confidence rather than emptiness. Avoid any decorative element, gradient wash, or icon — the only ornament is precision of alignment. The slide should feel typographically inevitable, as if no other arrangement of these words was ever possible.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with a 10% outer margin on all sides; the deck title anchors in the upper third, spanning cols 1–8, with a full-content-width hairline rule sitting immediately beneath it. A one-line subtitle or engagement framing sits below the rule in cols 1–6, creating deliberate right-side whitespace. Client name, date, and firm attribution are set flush-left at the bottom baseline, with no counterpart element on the right — the white void is intentional. No page number on the cover; hierarchy is enforced by vertical position and rule separation alone.

examples.promptCore: The slide projects the austere authority of a senior consulting deliverable — white-field, forensic, and unsparing. Mood is controlled confidence: the action title reads like a verdict handed down before testimony begins, and the three columns below function as parallel witnesses, each carrying equal rhetorical weight. Compositional rhythm is deliberately modular and symmetric — no column dominates, no visual ornament distracts, and the hairline rule acts as the sole dramatic separator between conclusion and evidence. Avoid warmth, depth effects, rounded shapes, or anything that softens the prosecutorial clarity of the layout.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with an 8% left/right outer margin and no header band. The declarative action-title sentence occupies a single full-width row (cols 1–12) immediately followed by a hairline rule that bleeds edge-to-edge between the margins. Below the rule, three symmetrical evidence columns occupy cols 1–4, 5–8, and 9–12 respectively; each column opens with a large upright numeral acting as an ordinal marker, then a concise column header, then two to four lines of body evidence copy. An 8pt italic source or attribution line is anchored flush-left at the bottom of the leftmost column, with a page number set flush-right at the same baseline.
